sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Apart from the pictures, do the type, colours and shapes share one mood and era, so the piece reads as one whole rather than a collage?** No.
   - **Where:** All eight bars (about x 177–1127, y 290–608) have a bevelled 3D look: a lighter top face and a darker right-hand side. That style looks like a default spreadsheet chart from the early 2000s.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** Everything around the chart is flat and current. That includes the serif headline, the clean sans text, the hairline gridlines, and the spaced capitals of the "PELLBROOK OUTDOOR" wordmark. A board member sees two eras on one slide, so the chart looks pasted in from an older deck rather than made for this one. That makes the review look less careful.
   - **Why:** The pieces don't share one way of drawing shapes. No approved source covers this; the catalog entries ("Thematic coherence: one mood, one era", "Unity: parts belong to one whole") are off the reading list. This is common sense: a board slide earns trust when it looks made as one piece.
   - **Fix:** Draw the bars flat, in the same style as the text and gridlines. Whoever reviews Charts and data should judge separately how the 3D extrusion makes the values harder to read.
   - Taste. Weight: minor. The slide still gets its point across; this costs polish and trust, not understanding.

**What's working.**
- **The headline makes a claim, and the chart proves it.** "Shipments peak each third quarter" is a statement, not just a label. The two tallest bars in each year (610 and 705) are both Q3, so a first-time viewer can say in one sentence what the slide is for and check it in a second.
- **Every supporting line has a job and names what it holds.** The subtitle gives the products, the time span, and the forecast caveat. The chart title and "Thousands of units" give the measure and the unit. The source line says where Q4 2026 comes from. A board reader is never left guessing what the numbers are.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (type, colours and shapes share one mood and era).

sections.report:
I ran this section without the crop and entries scripts because Bash was denied here. The image is about one screen (1280×800), so I worked from the whole image. I could not open the reference entries, so the one finding below is my own judgment and cites no catalog source.

**Section.** What matters first (hierarchy): applies.

**Findings**
1. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** No.
   - **Where:** The standfirst ("Tents, packs, and sleeping bags shipped…", about y 142) and the chart title ("Units shipped by quarter", about y 184) look the same size, roughly 16 px. One thing sets them apart: the standfirst is regular mid-grey and the chart title is bold near-black. So the chart title, which sits lower, carries more weight than the line that explains the headline. Under the chart title, three small grey lines look like one level, about 13–14 px each: "Thousands of units" (y 209), the running header at top right (y 35) and the source line (y 671). The units line is part of how you read the chart, but it looks the same as the page furniture.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** After the headline, the eye goes to the bold chart title before the standfirst, so it reads in the wrong order. Most readers will also read past the unit ("thousands") because it looks like boilerplate, and then the bar values (410, 705) have no scale.
   - **Why:** Common sense and taste. I could not read the catalog entries for this line, so I don't cite them.
   - **Fix:** Settle the order between the standfirst and the chart title. Either make the standfirst clearly the second level (darker, or a step larger) and the chart title a quieter label, or tie the chart title and the units into one block that stays below the standfirst. Move the unit into the chart title ("Units shipped by quarter, thousands") so it doesn't share a style with the footer and header.
   - **Type and weight:** Taste, minor.

**What's working.**
- The headline "Shipments peak each third quarter" (y 98, about 34 px bold serif) clearly dominates the page. It is the only serif, about twice the size of anything else, and the darkest text. The eye knows where to start, and it reads as the claim the page makes.
- The headline is set apart in more than size: serif against sans, bold, and near-black against the grey supporting text. You never confuse it with the chart title, even though both are bold.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (each text level distinct from the next).

sections.report:
I walked the "Arrangement and space" section of the checklist on this image. The entries script and the crop script both need Bash, which was refused, so I worked from the whole image (about 1280×800, one screen) and read the entries straight from `references/layout.md`.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is the space inside each group clearly smaller than the space between groups, so each heading sits nearer the text it introduces?** No. The chart heading "Units shipped by quarter" and "Thousands of units" (y≈177–215) sit about 27 px below the page subtitle (which ends at y≈150). They sit about 40 px above the top of the chart (the "800" label, y≈259). So the chart's own heading reads as the end of the intro block, not as the label of the chart, and the unit ("thousands") comes loose from the numbers it qualifies. The source is Arnheim's proximity rule, "Space shows the groups": a label sits nearer its own field than the one before it. Fix: open the gap above the chart heading and close the gap between "Thousands of units" and the plot, so the heading, the unit and the chart read as one group. **Defect**, minor.
2. **Do all blocks, pictures included, take their edges and the gaps between them from one grid, so column lines and gutters repeat down the page?** No. The header, headline, subtitle, chart heading, footer rule and source line all use left 80 and right 1200. The chart does not:
   - its y-axis labels start at about x 115;
   - its plot and gridlines run from about 150 to 1140;
   - the baseline stops 60 px short of the 1200 edge that the footer rule right below it reaches.

   The chart, which is the main block, therefore looks placed by eye inside the page's column instead of filling it. This is most visible on the right, where the gridlines end short of the header text "…October board meeting" and of the footer rule. The source is Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*, "One grid governs the page". Fix: run the plot to the same right edge (1200), and either hang the axis labels in the left margin so the plot starts at 80, or align the labels to 80. **Convention**, minor.
3. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** No. All the content ends at the footer (y≈680), leaving an empty band about 110 px tall (about 14% of the frame) across the whole bottom. Above it sit the dense dark bars, so the page looks top-heavy and cut short, like a 16:9 slide dropped into a taller frame. The source is Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, "Balance": a heavy part needs a counterweight. Fix: give the chart the leftover height, or centre the content block vertically, so the space is shared out top and bottom rather than dumped at the bottom. If this band only comes from how the screenshot was taken, it is not a finding. **Defect** (mild), minor.

**What's working.**
- One strong left edge at x 80 holds the brand, headline, subtitle, chart heading and source line. With the flush-left setting, it gives a clear top-down reading order with no centring habit.
- The header and footer mirror each other: label on the left, meta on the right, on shared baselines, with a hairline rule above the footer. This frames the page quietly and keeps the meta text out of the way of the headline and chart.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the empty bottom band is in the slide itself or comes from the capture viewport. Check it in the source deck at its real aspect ratio.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 10 yes, 3 no (one grid; space shows the groups; balance)

**Section.** Text: applies. The image is a single 1280×800 slide with a headline, a deck, a chart title, axis and value labels, a header and a footer. I could not run the crop script because Bash was not allowed, so I judged everything from the whole image, which is about one screen.

**Findings**
None.

These two copy points have no checklist line, so they are not counted in the tally. They are here for the director to weigh:
- **Copy, minor (taste):** The deck at about y 142 says "Q4 2026" twice in one line: "eight quarters to Q4 2026 (Q4 2026 is the forecast)". It reads like a patch added after the line was written. A tighter version is "…eight quarters from Q1 2025; Q4 2026 is a forecast." The footer at y 671 already repeats the forecast note.
- **Copy, minor (taste):** The headline at y 98 is "Shipments peak each third quarter". It states a seasonal pattern that rests on only two cycles. It also leaves out the second thing the chart shows: each 2026 quarter is above the same quarter of 2025, with Q3 going from 610 to 705. A board audience will want that growth. The headline could carry both, for example "Shipments peak each Q3, and 2026 is running ahead of 2025." This overlaps the whole and hierarchy sections, so the director should decide where it goes.

**What's working.**
- **Clear type plan.** There is one bold serif for the headline and one plain sans for everything else. The steps between sizes are distinct: headline, then deck, then chart title, then axis and source text. The weight change on "Units shipped by quarter" sets it apart from its unit line "Thousands of units" without adding another size.
- **Careful small text.** The all-caps brand name "PELLBROOK OUTDOOR" (top left) is letterspaced. The deck and the header are mixed case. Small grey text, such as the axis labels, the source line and "Page 3 of 12", looks dark enough and heavy enough to read. To confirm, the grey of the footer is the value to measure for 4.5:1 contrast.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

**Section.** Color: applies. The page has colour outside the chart: the navy wordmark, the dark title, the grey supporting text, the hairline rules and the white ground.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The palette is tight.** The page uses one neutral range (near-black title, mid-grey subtitle and source line, pale grey rules, white ground) and one blue family, which runs from the navy "PELLBROOK OUTDOOR" wordmark at top left (about 80–270, 28–42 px) to the mid-blue bars. Nothing on the page competes for attention, so all the colour weight goes to the data. Keep it to this one hue.
- **Light and dark carry the structure.** The near-black serif title (about 80–660, 80–118 px) is the darkest text, the grey subtitle, chart subtitle and source line step down from it, and the white ground keeps the page open. In grayscale the reading order would still be title, chart, then the small print. Hold onto this range of light and dark when revising.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

I could only look at the whole image. The crop script never ran because shell commands were refused, so I didn't inspect any detail at full resolution. The image is about one screen, so it may not have needed cutting.

There are two colour problems inside the chart, which this section leaves out. They belong to the `data` critic, and the director should check that report covers them. First, the Q4 2026 bar is a forecast but is drawn in the same blue as the actual quarters. Second, the headline says shipments peak each third quarter, but no colour picks out the Q3 bars.

First read: the eye lands on the serif headline, then on the tallest bar (Q3 2026, 705). It's a board-meeting sales slide with one chart.

Walk (Pictures):
- Applies only through the "PELLBROOK OUTDOOR" wordmark at the top left (~80–270, 27–42). There are no photos, illustrations or icons. The 3D extruded bars are fake depth, but they are chart marks, so they belong under Charts and data and not here.
- Content shown, no broken image: yes
- Full quality: yes
- Crops intended: yes (no crops)
- Figure-ground: yes
- One rendering style: yes
- Photos consistent: yes (none)
- Icon strokes consistent: yes (none)
- One viewpoint and light: yes (no scene; the bars go to Charts and data)
- Texture restrained: yes
- No fake depth: yes for pictures (the 3D bars go to Charts and data)
- Logo clear space, undistorted, own colours: yes
- Logo simple, one colour: yes

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so I don't need to open any entries.

**Section.** Pictures: applies, but only through the "PELLBROOK OUTDOOR" wordmark. There are no photos, illustrations or icons.

**Findings**
None.

Note for the director: the bars are drawn in 3D, with a lit top face and a dark side face (all eight bars, x ≈ 177–1127, y ≈ 290–608). That is fake depth. I left it out of this section because the checklist says chart defects are filed under Charts and data. The data critic should report it there: the 3D tops make each bar's height ambiguous against the gridlines and add decoration that carries no data.

**What's working.** The wordmark is set in spaced, bold, dark-blue capitals with plenty of empty space around it. It reads clearly at small size in one colour, and its blue matches the bars, which ties the brand to the chart without adding a logo graphic.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 12 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes): Charts and data**
First read: the eye goes to the serif headline, then to the tallest bar (Q3 2026, 705). The 3D blocks look heavy and like stock clip-art.
1. Form fits: yes (bars for eight discrete quarters)
2. Series followable: yes (one series)
3. Ink is data, no 3D: **no**. All eight bars are extruded 3D blocks with lit top faces and dark side faces.
4. Honest scales: yes (starts at 0, ticks every 200)
5. Enough time range: **no**. "Each third quarter" rests on two Q3s, one of them partly forecast-era.
6. Palette fits data: yes
7. Readable without colour vision: yes
8. Few colours, emphasis: **no**. The title's claim is about Q3, but the Q3 bars look the same as the others.
9. Direct labels: yes
10. Axis values, units, labels: yes ("Thousands of units")
11. Labels clear: yes
12. Title states the finding: yes
13. Natural order: yes (chronological)
14. Forecast marked: **no**. The Q4 2026 bar looks exactly like the actual bars.
15. Headline number has comparison: yes (no standalone figure)
16. Dashboard on one screen: yes (n/a)

---

**Section.** Charts and data: applies (one single-series bar chart of units shipped by quarter).

**Findings**
1. **Is each estimate or forecast marked as one, by a range or a different line style?** The Q4 2026 bar (x ≈ 1043–1127, y ≈ 355–608) has the same solid blue, 3D treatment and bold "560" label as the seven actual quarters. The only signs that it's a forecast are the subtitle's parenthetical (y ≈ 142) and the source line (y ≈ 671). A board member scanning the chart reads 560 as something that happened. They could also take Q3→Q4 2026 as a confirmed drop, or treat 560 vs 480 as a real year-on-year gain. Few and Wilke both say forecasts should look different from actuals. **Fix:** give the Q4 2026 bar its own look (outline only, a lighter tint or hatching) and label it on the chart ("560 forecast"), ideally with a range. **Defect. Major.**
2. **Is nearly all the ink in each chart data, with no 3D, shadows, textures, or heavy gridlines?** Every bar has a lit top face and a dark side face that add depth with no meaning. The top faces rise above the true value, so the eye can't tell whether the front edge or the back edge marks the number. The value labels sit above the cap, not at the value. It also makes a board document look like a default spreadsheet chart, which costs credibility. Source: Tufte, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information* (data-ink, chartjunk). **Fix:** use flat 2D bars. The value labels are already there, so the gridlines could also be lighter or removed. **Convention, with a small accuracy cost. Major**, because it's the main visual impression of the chart and fixing it is cheap.
3. **Does each chart use few distinct colors for its series or categories, with gray for context?** The headline says shipments peak each third quarter, but all eight bars are the same blue. The reader has to find the Q3 bars (x ≈ 425 and 920) by reading the axis labels. **Fix:** colour Q3 2025 and Q3 2026 in the accent and put the other quarters in a muted tint or grey, so the chart proves the title at a glance. Few and Wilke both recommend using colour for emphasis. **Convention. Minor**, though it would noticeably sharpen the chart's one point.
4. **Does each chart show enough of the time range or sample to judge the trend?** "Peak each third quarter" is drawn from two cycles, 2025 and 2026. Two peaks is the least evidence that can show a pattern, and the second year's Q4 is a forecast. A board member could fairly ask whether this is seasonality or two coincidences. **Fix:** show a third year (or more) if the data exists, or soften the claim to "Q3 was the peak in both years". **Common sense (the catalog entry has no approved source). Minor.**

**What's working.**
- The title states the finding ("Shipments peak each third quarter"), and the chart title and unit line ("Units shipped by quarter / Thousands of units") name the measure and the scale cleanly. The reader never has to guess what a bar means.
- The axis starts at zero with even 200-unit ticks, and each bar is labelled directly. Exact values are readable without a gridline lookup, and bar lengths are honest.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: 16 lines, 12 yes, 4 no (forecast marked; no 3D/chartjunk; colour used for emphasis; enough time range), 0 unsure

**Section.** Interface: skipped. This is a static board-report slide (a title, a subtitle, a 3D bar chart, a source line and a page number). It has no buttons, links, fields, menus or navigation.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Interface: skipped
